title: "4.17 Async FastAPI with async SQLAlchemy"
description: "Measure when a thread pool runs out, convert Atlas's API and its tests to async database access, keep CPU-heavy work off the event loop, and catch the lazy-loading trap of async ORMs with a test."

::: {.lesson-meta}
Part 4 · Lesson 17 · About 2 hours
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Analogy: one waiter, many tables"}
A restaurant can hire one waiter per table, who stands beside it while the kitchen cooks (threads). Or one waiter can serve twenty tables: take an order, hand it to the kitchen, and serve other tables until the kitchen calls (async). The single waiter is efficient only if they never stand still waiting: a waiter who personally cooks a slow dish (blocking work) leaves every other table unattended.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Minimum path"}
Read "The problem", "Theory" and "In the project". The trade-offs section *(deep dive)* helps you decide whether a project of your own should be async at all.
:::

## The problem

Atlas's routes have been plain `def`, because SQLAlchemy's `Session` is synchronous: every query blocks its thread until Postgres answers. Lesson 4.1 showed that FastAPI runs `def` routes in a **thread pool** so a blocking call holds up only its own thread. But a pool has a size. Starlette's default allows 40 threads to run route code at once.

Atlas's queries take milliseconds, so 40 is plenty today. Part 6 changes that: answering a question means waiting several seconds for a language model, and Part 5's worker waits on GitHub. Here is a small app with two routes that each wait one second, one the `def` way and one the `async def` way, and many requests arriving at once:

```python
@app.get("/sync-wait")
def sync_wait() -> dict[str, str]:
    time.sleep(1)  # a slow call that blocks: a synchronous HTTP client or database driver
    return {"waited": "1s in a worker thread"}


@app.get("/async-wait")
async def async_wait() -> dict[str, str]:
    await asyncio.sleep(1)  # the same wait, awaited
    return {"waited": "1s on the event loop"}
```
```text
40 requests to /sync-wait: 1.1s
200 requests to /sync-wait: 5.7s
40 requests to /async-wait: 1.1s
200 requests to /async-wait: 1.7s
```

Up to 40 at once, both are the same. At 200, the `def` route took five times as long: requests queued for the 40 threads, which worked through them in five rounds of one second. The `async def` route kept all 200 waits in flight on one thread. With multi-second model calls, that queue is the difference between an app that works and one that times out.

## Theory

Lesson 2.6 introduced `async`/`await` and the **event loop**; lesson 4.1 measured what happens when an `async def` route blocks. Converting Atlas means:

- database calls through SQLAlchemy's async layer, awaited;
- outgoing HTTP calls (GitHub sign-in) through an async client, awaited;
- CPU-heavy work (password hashing) handed to the thread pool;
- tests that call the app asynchronously too.

Part 6 streams LLM answers that take many seconds each, and the WebSocket in lesson 4.18 holds a connection open indefinitely. Both are long *waits*, exactly what async is good at. The cost: everything slow must be awaited, and a single blocking call stalls everyone.

### Async SQLAlchemy

SQLAlchemy has an async layer with the same ideas and new names:

| Synchronous (4.1 to 4.16) | Async (4.17 on) |
|---|---|
| `create_engine(url)` | `create_async_engine(url)` |
| `sessionmaker(engine)` | `async_sessionmaker(engine)` |
| `Session` | `AsyncSession` |
| `session.execute(...)` | `await session.execute(...)` |
| `session.commit()` | `await session.commit()` |
| `with factory() as session` | `async with factory() as session` |

The URL stays `postgresql+psycopg://...`: psycopg 3 supports both modes. Install the extra that async SQLAlchemy needs: `uv add "sqlalchemy[asyncio]"` (it brings the `greenlet` package, which SQLAlchemy uses internally to bridge the two styles).

`session.add(obj)` stays synchronous: it only puts an object in the session's memory, without talking to the database.

### The lazy-loading trap

With a synchronous session, touching `issue.repo` on an issue whose repository isn't loaded quietly runs a query (a **lazy load**). In async code, a query must be awaited, and an attribute access can't be. So SQLAlchemy refuses:

```text
sqlalchemy.exc.MissingGreenlet: greenlet_spawn has not been called; can't call await_() here. Was IO attempted in an unexpected place? (Background on this error at: https://sqlalche.me/e/21/xd2s)
```

That's what you get running `issue = await session.get(Issue, 1)` and then `issue.repo.full_name`. The fix is to say up front what to load: `selectinload(Issue.repo)` (lesson 4.12). It also kills N+1 queries, so async forces a good habit. And `expire_on_commit=False` matters more now: after a commit, expired attributes would also need a reload.

### CPU-heavy work

Argon2 (lesson 4.7) takes about 0.06 s of pure computation. Nothing to await, so in an `async def` route it would block the loop for every login. Starlette's `run_in_threadpool(func, *args)` runs a blocking function in the thread pool and lets you await the result.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  L[event loop] -->|await session.execute| PG[(Postgres)]
  PG -->|rows| L
  L -->|await run_in_threadpool| T[worker thread<br/>Argon2 hash]
  T -->|result| L
  L -.->|meanwhile| O[other requests]
```

## In the project

The conversion touched every route file, `deps.py`, `app.py` and `github_oauth.py`, and nothing outside `api/`, because the CLI keeps its synchronous code. Here's the shape of the change.

### Engine and sessions

```python
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import async_sessionmaker, create_async_engine

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    engine = create_async_engine(settings.database_url, pool_pre_ping=True)
    # expire_on_commit=False: objects stay readable after commit without a surprise reload,
    # which in async code would be an implicit (and forbidden) database call.
    app.state.session_factory = async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False)
    yield
    await engine.dispose()
```

`deps.py`, as a diff (lines starting `-` were removed, `+` added):

```diff
-def get_session(request: Request) -> Iterator[Session]:
+async def get_session(request: Request) -> AsyncIterator[AsyncSession]:
     """One database session per request, always closed, even if the route raises."""
-    with request.app.state.session_factory() as session:
+    async with request.app.state.session_factory() as session:
         yield session

-SessionDep = Annotated[Session, Depends(get_session)]
+SessionDep = Annotated[AsyncSession, Depends(get_session)]

-def get_current_user(
+async def get_current_user(
     ...
-    user = session.get(User, user_id)
+    user = await session.get(User, user_id)
```

Because routes depend on `SessionDep` and `CurrentUser` by name, their signatures don't change.

### A route

```diff
 @router.patch("/me", response_model=UserOut)
-def update_me(changes: UserUpdate, user: CurrentUser, session: SessionDep) -> User:
+async def update_me(changes: UserUpdate, user: CurrentUser, session: SessionDep) -> User:
     for field, value in changes.model_dump(exclude_unset=True).items():
         setattr(user, field, value)
-    session.commit()
-    session.refresh(user)
+    await session.commit()
+    await session.refresh(user)
     return user
```

Most of the conversion is this mechanical. mypy (lesson 1.11) catches the places you forget: a forgotten `await` leaves a coroutine where a value was expected.

### Hashing off the loop

```python
from starlette.concurrency import run_in_threadpool

@router.post("/register", status_code=status.HTTP_201_CREATED, response_model=UserOut)
async def register(body: UserCreate, session: SessionDep) -> User:
    password_hash = await run_in_threadpool(hash_password, body.password)
    user = User(email=body.email, password_hash=password_hash)
    ...
```

`login` does the same for both `verify_password` calls.

### Calling GitHub without blocking

`github_oauth.exchange_code` now uses `httpx.AsyncClient`, httpx's async twin, and is itself `async def`:

```python
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10.0, transport=transport) as client:
        token_response = await client.post(TOKEN_URL, data={...}, headers={"Accept": "application/json"})
        ...
        user_response = await client.get(f"{GITHUB_API}/user", headers={...})
```

### Red, then green: the lazy load the tests missed

`get_issue_or_404` reads `issue.repo.full_name` (through `issue_out`), so it must load the repository up front with `selectinload(Issue.repo)`. In the synchronous version a missing option was a silent extra query; in the async version it's a 500. Yet when the option was missing, the whole test suite still passed. Why? The tests stored their sample issues through the same session the route then used, and that session still held the `Repo` object in memory, so no query was needed. A fresh request in production starts with an empty session.

The test that would have caught it says exactly that:

```python
async def test_reading_an_issue_loads_everything_it_needs(
    client: httpx.AsyncClient, async_session: AsyncSession
) -> None:
    """Async code can't load relationships lazily (lesson 4.17), so the route must ask up front.

    expunge_all() empties the session's memory of objects, as a fresh request's session
    would be; without it, the repository loaded while storing would hide a missing load.
    """
    ids = await store_numbers(async_session, [7])
    async_session.expunge_all()

    response = await client.get(f"/issues/{ids[7]}")

    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert response.json()["repo"] == "pytorch/ignite"
```

Without `selectinload(Issue.repo)`:

```text
E           sqlalchemy.exc.MissingGreenlet: greenlet_spawn has not been called; can't call await_() here. Was IO attempted in an unexpected place? (Background on this error at: https://sqlalche.me/e/21/xd2s)
```

With it, the test passes. The general lesson: a test's setup can make a bug invisible. Ask "what does the real situation have that my test doesn't?" (here: an empty session).

### Converting the tests

The routes are `async def` now, so the tests call the app asynchronously too, with three changes in `tests/conftest.py`.

**Async tests.** The **anyio** pytest plugin (installed with FastAPI) runs `async def` tests; each test module opts in with `pytestmark = pytest.mark.anyio`, and a fixture picks the event loop:

```python
@pytest.fixture
def anyio_backend() -> str:
    # Async tests run on asyncio, the event loop FastAPI and SQLAlchemy use.
    return "asyncio"
```

**An async rolled-back session**, the same idea as lesson 4.5's, with async names:

```python
@pytest.fixture
async def async_session(engine: Engine) -> AsyncIterator[AsyncSession]:
    """Like the `session` fixture, but async: one transaction, rolled back after the test.

    Depends on `engine` so the tables exist (and so the test is skipped without a database).
    NullPool: a fresh connection per test, created on this test's own event loop.
    """
    async_engine = create_async_engine(
        str(engine.url.render_as_string(hide_password=False)), poolclass=NullPool
    )
    async with async_engine.connect() as connection:
        transaction = await connection.begin()
        session = AsyncSession(
            bind=connection, join_transaction_mode="create_savepoint", expire_on_commit=False
        )
        try:
            yield session
        finally:
            await session.close()
            await transaction.rollback()
    await async_engine.dispose()
```

`NullPool` matters here: each test runs on its own event loop, and a pooled async connection from one loop can't be reused on another.

**An async client.** `httpx.AsyncClient` with an `ASGITransport` calls the app in-process, like `TestClient` did, but awaitably:

```python
def browser(app: FastAPI) -> httpx.AsyncClient:
    """A client with its own cookies, like a separate browser (lesson 4.9's attacks need two)."""
    return httpx.AsyncClient(transport=httpx.ASGITransport(app=app), base_url="http://test")
```

and every test changes the same mechanical way: `def` becomes `async def`, `client.get(...)` becomes `await client.get(...)`. `ASGITransport` doesn't run the app's lifespan, which is fine: the session override supplies the database.

Tests that need data from `storage.py`, which stays synchronous because the command line uses it, run it on the async session's connection with `run_sync`:

```python
async def store_issues(session: AsyncSession, issues: list[github.Issue]) -> dict[int, int]:
    await session.run_sync(lambda sync: storage.save_issues(sync, "pytorch/ignite", issues))
    await session.commit()
    rows = await session.execute(select(Issue.number, Issue.id))
    return {number: issue_id for number, issue_id in rows}
```

### Results

```text
$ uv run pytest -q
...
124 passed in 9.90s
```

The behaviour is identical, so every test from the synchronous version passes, converted. All the curl output in lessons 4.1 to 4.16 was in fact captured from the async version.

## Trade-offs: should a project be async? *(deep dive)*

| Situation | Better choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Short database queries, modest traffic | plain `def` | simpler; the thread pool is never the bottleneck |
| Many slow waits at once (LLM calls, other APIs, long polls) | `async def` | waits don't hold threads, as measured above |
| WebSockets or streaming responses | `async def` | the connection stays open for a long time |
| Heavy computation per request | neither alone | move it to a worker process (Part 5) or the thread pool |
| A library you need has no async version | `def`, or `run_in_threadpool` around it | one blocking call in `async def` stalls everything |

Mixing is allowed: FastAPI runs each route the way it's declared. But a codebase where half the routes are async and half aren't makes every reader ask "is this one safe to block?". Atlas converts everything at once, in one lesson, for that reason.

## Common mistakes

- **A synchronous call in an async route**: `requests.get`, `time.sleep`, a sync `Session`, Argon2 without `run_in_threadpool`. Everything stalls.
- **Forgetting `await`**: you get a coroutine object instead of a result. Type checking catches most of these.
- **Lazy loading** (`MissingGreenlet`). Load relationships with `selectinload` in the query.
- **Sharing one `AsyncSession` between concurrent tasks** (for example in `asyncio.gather`). One session per task.
- **Converting for its own sake.** A sync API in a thread pool is fine for many apps. Switch when you need many concurrent waits, as Atlas does from Part 6.

## Check yourself

**1.** Why does `session.add(user)` have no `await`, while `session.commit()` does?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`add` only registers the object in the session's memory; no database work happens. `commit` sends SQL and waits for Postgres, which is I/O, so it's awaited.
:::

**2.** What does `MissingGreenlet` usually mean in an async FastAPI app?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Code touched a relationship (or an expired attribute) that wasn't loaded, so SQLAlchemy needed to query the database in a place that can't be awaited. Load it up front with `selectinload` (or `await session.refresh(obj, ["relationship"])`).
:::

**3.** Hashing a password involves no I/O. Why does it still go through `run_in_threadpool`?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It's 0.06 s of CPU work. Run directly in an async route, it would hold the event loop for that time on every login, delaying every other request. In a worker thread, the loop keeps serving others.
:::

## Exercise

Write a small async script that opens an `AsyncSession` on your dev database and prints the titles of the three newest issues with their labels, without triggering `MissingGreenlet`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```python
import asyncio

from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import async_sessionmaker, create_async_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import selectinload

from atlas.models import Issue

URL = "postgresql+psycopg://atlas:atlas-dev-password@localhost:5432/atlas"


async def main() -> None:
    engine = create_async_engine(URL)
    async with async_sessionmaker(engine)() as session:
        statement = (
            select(Issue).order_by(Issue.number.desc()).limit(3)
            .options(selectinload(Issue.labels))
        )
        for issue in await session.scalars(statement):
            print(issue.title, [label.name for label in issue.labels])
    await engine.dispose()


asyncio.run(main())
```
Remove `.options(...)` to see `MissingGreenlet`.
:::

## Stretch

Find blocking calls automatically: run a test app containing an `async def` route that calls `time.sleep(1)` with Python's asyncio **debug mode** switched on (`PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 uv run uvicorn ...`), call that route and an awaiting one, and read the server's output.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Debug mode makes the event loop report any single step that holds it for longer than 0.1 seconds. Only the blocking route is reported:

```text
Executing <Task finished name='Task-3' coro=<RequestResponseCycle.run_asgi() done, defined at .../uvicorn/protocols/http/httptools_impl.py:420> result=None ...> took 1.002 seconds
```

The awaiting route waits just as long but gives the loop back, so it isn't. Debug mode slows everything down, so it's a development tool, not a production setting.
:::

## What changed in the project

All API routes and dependencies are `async def` on `AsyncSession`; `github_oauth.exchange_code` is async; password hashing runs in the thread pool; the tests use `anyio`, `async_session` and an async client; a regression test for lazy loads. `sqlalchemy[asyncio]` added. Commits: `feat: Converted the Atlas API to async`, `test: Caught routes that rely on lazy loading, which async sessions can't do`.
